messages.body_plain:
Dear collegues,

I am a bit stuck in an analytical procedure and maybe you could provide me some light…

I have a zigzag equally spaced survey and would like to apply a correction for overlapping corners where two transects meet (areas surveyed twice). I would like to apply a correction to the total coverage area to account for the double-counting effort and avoid potential bias. I have seen in a previous analysis that you can add it as multiplier called “overlap” within Distance software, for example, but I dont know how to estimate the number that goes in there. I guess I should entre my shape file or coordinates with the tracks/transects somewhere first and define my truncation distance. I also use R, so if you think it´s easier with a package function.

Thanks a lot in advance!

Daniel

messages.body_plain:
Daniel

I am not acquainted with analyses that have used a multiplier for zigzag surveys to address overlapping coverage at the end of transects. Depending upon the size of your study area, I would expect this area to be small. Compound the small size of overlap with a detection probability <1, implying the likelihood of double-counting is pretty small. I would think this would be a second- or third-order problem for your analysis. Maybe I'm wrong, but I would think this area of overlap would be <5% for many study areas. Double counting is seldom a first-order problem in distance sampling surveys unless animals are being "driven" from one transect to the next. Good field procedures can further minimise the issue.

See slide 6 of this online lecture:
https://workshops.distancesampling.org/online-course/lecturepdfs/Ch2/L2-3%20Making%20Distance%20Sampling%20Work.pdf

messages.body_plain:
Suzika

Thanks for your question. The short answer to your question about the warning message: you did not give the appropriate name to the field that specifies the labels for the transects. You need to name the field "Sample.Label" rather than "LineTransect.Label". When doing that, the warning message goes away.

SLdata <- read.csv("E:/troubleshoot/Suzy/Mammal_recce survey.csv")
colnames(SLdata)[3] <- "Sample.Label"

But I think you have more problems than that. Your data indicate you have two strata (AD and CA), but there is only a single transect in each stratum. That is a design that does not permit estimation of variability between transects; it will be difficult to make inference from such a design.

Second, there are only 19 detections in the data set; that will be difficult for detection function fitting. However, those 19 detections are spread among 6 species, further diminishing the number of detections per species (I doubt that deer and squirrels share the same detection function).

Finally, I don't know the units in which effort and perpendicular detection distance is measured, but I suspect there is a problem with the recorded distance measurements. 17 of the 19 detections have recorded detection distance of 0.1, one detection distance of 0.5 and another detection distance of 20. Fitting a detection function will not be possible to data such as that; it does not appear that detectability is a function of distance for those data.

messages.body_plain:
Hello colleagues! As part of my PhD thesis I'm working on some dsm for a dolphin species in southern Argentina. I'm having trouble calculating the variance estimation, I keep receiving an error. I was doing it with the following code:

preddata.varprop <- split(prediction.data, 1:nrow(prediction.data))
dsm.xy.varprop <- dsm_var_prop(model1, pred.data = preddata.varprop,
                               off.set = prediction.data$AREA)
summary(dsm.xy.varprop)

This is what came out from the code:
Error in dsm_var_prop(modelo.t14, pred.data = preddata.varprop, off.set = prediction.data2$AREA) :
No detection function in this analysis, use dsm_var_gam

I changed to dsm_var_gam and I got this:

> summary(dsm.xy.varprop)
Summary of uncertainty in a density surface model calculated
 analytically for GAM, with delta method
Approximate asymptotic confidence interval:
      2.5%       Mean      97.5%
  45.63008  360.08097 2841.50936
(Using log-Normal approximation)
Point estimate                 : 360.081

Error in round(x$gam.cv <http://gam.cv/>, 4) :
  non-numeric argument to mathematical function

I keep receiving that error, do you have an idea of how to correct it?
My selected model has a tweedie distribution and three covariates:

model1 <- dsm(count~s(x,y, k=15)+s(distcosta, k=10)+s(rug, k=10),dummy_ddf(observation.data$object,width=600),segment.data,observation.data,family=tw(), method="REML")

Many thanks in advance

Aymeric

I have had a brief look at the radial detection distances in the spreadsheet you provided. You will have difficulty fitting a detection function to the data for a few reasons:
point transect data are inherently difficult to which to fit detections function models,
the number of detections per site is small (presumably you wish to produce estimates at the site level) and
there is considerable round of distances to favoured distances (10, 15, 20, 25m) see below
I note that not all of your sites had 45 points: Bakas and Tegallalang  had 46, Hengkulak and Ubud had 36, Bali Barat and Uluwatu had 9, Candidasa had 11 and Mekori had 1.
It is difficult to know (because of the huge number of detections around 10m) whether detectability is perfect to that distance or whether rounding is influencing the shape of the fitted detection function.
Estimated numbers of macaques from these models is extremely large (in the tens of thousands for some sites); you must determine if those numbers are biologically plausible.
As for your comment about analysing data as detections of clusters or detections of individuals, the results produced should be similar from the two approaches. Using detections of individuals, there is not the challenge of estimating the distance to the centre of the group, nor estimating the group size.

messages.body_plain:
Kammie

When using a continuous covariate in the detection function using Distance for Windows software, here is the description of the plot taken from Chapter 9 of the Users Guide:
>
> Plot: Example Detection Functions. If there are any non-factor covariates, then the above plots show the detection function (or pdf) averaged over the observed covariate levels. Depending on the observed covariates, the shape of these functions can be quite different from the detection function given fixed covariate values. So, for each non-factor covariate, the MCDS engine outputs a plot showing 3 example detection functions. These are evaluated at the 25th, 50th and 75th quartiles of the covariate. If there is more than one non-factor covariate, the values of the other covariates are fixed at the 50th percentile.

If you wish to duplicate the plot in R, there is a function  add_df_covar_line()​. An example of its use can be found in one of our online vignettes:

http://examples.distancesampling.org/Distance-spec-covar/species-covariate-distill.html

Hope that helps.

Zhilin Li

The issue of population closure in camera trap studies must be considered regardless of the analysis method. The use of spatial capture-recapture methodology (except those that assume some form of movement model, see Efford and Schofield 2022 below) similarly employs the closure assumption.  This has been described for some time, as an example see the following:
Marnewick, K., Funston, P. J., & Karanth, K. U. (2008). Evaluating camera trapping as a method for estimating cheetah abundance in ranching areas. South African Journal of Wildlife Research 38(1), 59-65.
Citation for open SCR models
Efford, M. G., & Schofield, M. R. (2022). A review of movement models in open population capture–recapture. Methods in Ecology and Evolution,  13, 2106–  2118.  https://doi.org/10.1111/2041-210X.13947
With CTDS, the estimate of density produced is an average of the density of the population in the area over the duration of the data collection period. The utility of that average estimate is dependent upon the amount of population change over that period.

Hope that is helpful.
